module.title: Introduction to Division
module.subtitle: Equal sharing, equal groups, and making sense of leftovers
module.subject: Mathematics
module.attribution: Jonathan's Creative Archive Contributors; original division lesson drafted with Codex assistance, 2026
learning_objectives: Explain the difference between sharing a total among a known number of groups and making groups of a known size.
Read a division sentence and identify the dividend, divisor, and quotient.
Solve whole-number division problems using objects, repeated subtraction, or multiplication facts and check the result.
Find a whole-number quotient and remainder, then interpret them in a story.
Explain why zero divided by a positive number is zero and division by zero is undefined.

prerequisites.title: Basic Addition and Subtraction
prerequisites.description: Count items and subtract equal groups. Larger totals in this lesson can be handled with objects or repeated addition.

prerequisites.title: Introduction to Multiplication
prerequisites.description: Understand equal groups and multiplication facts; memorizing all facts is not required.

introduction.plain_text:
# Why Division Matters

Suppose a group is setting up a shared workshop. There are twelve pencils and three tables. How many pencils can each table receive if every table gets the same number? Division helps answer questions about equal groups.

Sometimes you know how many groups you want, such as three tables. Sometimes you know the size of each group, such as four pencils in each supply bag, and want to find how many bags you can fill. Both are division questions, but the answer describes something different.

You can explore with marks on paper, familiar objects, or just the written descriptions here. You do not need to answer quickly or memorize every multiplication fact. We will connect division to multiplication, check answers, and explain what to do when items are left over. These ideas help with sharing supplies, arranging materials, and preparing to learn fractions.

sections.title: Section 1: Equal Sharing and Equal Groups
sections.content:
# Two Questions, One Operation

Division starts with a total and asks about equal groups. Here we use whole numbers: zero, one, two, and so on. Our objects stay whole; cutting them into fractions comes later.

In equal sharing, you know the number of groups. Share twelve counters among three trays. Give one counter to each tray, then repeat until all twelve are used. Each tray receives four counters. The answer is four counters per tray.

In equal grouping, you know the size of each group. Put twelve counters into groups of three counters. You can make four groups. The answer is four groups, rather than four counters per tray. Naming what the answer counts helps you distinguish these questions.

Both calculations are written 12 ÷ 3 = 4, read as “twelve divided by three equals four.” The dividend is the total being divided: twelve. The divisor tells the number of groups or their size: three. The quotient is the result: four. You may also see 12 / 3; the slash means division here.

A text picture of the sharing example is: tray A has four counters, tray B has four, and tray C has four. There are three equal groups and twelve counters altogether.

Multiplication checks division: three groups of four make twelve, so 3 × 4 = 12 confirms 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Division undoes equal-group multiplication. Changing the order usually changes the answer: 12 ÷ 3 and 3 ÷ 12 are different questions.

sections.title: Section 2: Checking Remainders and Handling Zero
sections.content:
# Leftovers Have Meaning

You can divide by subtracting equal groups. To find 14 ÷ 4, subtract four repeatedly: fourteen becomes ten, then six, then two. You removed three full groups. The two items left form the remainder. Write “14 ÷ 4 = 3 remainder 2.” This is whole-number division with a leftover, not the claim that 14 ÷ 4 equals exactly 3.

Check with multiplication and addition: total = divisor × whole-number quotient + remainder. Here, 14 = 4 × 3 + 2. For a positive whole-number divisor, the remainder must be at least zero and smaller than the divisor. A remainder of four would allow another full group. Exact division has remainder zero.

Read the story before choosing the final answer. Four people sharing fourteen whole counters receive three each with two left. Boxes holding at most four counters require four boxes to store all fourteen: three full boxes and one partly filled box. The calculation is the same; the requested answer differs. Neither answer means discarding the leftover items.

Zero items shared among four groups gives zero in each: 0 ÷ 4 = 0, checked by 4 × 0 = 0. Dividing a number by one leaves that number unchanged.

Division by zero is undefined in ordinary arithmetic. For 8 ÷ 0, no number multiplied by zero gives eight. For 0 ÷ 0, every number multiplied by zero gives zero, so multiplication does not identify a unique answer. We therefore leave both expressions undefined. Zero divided by a positive number is allowed; a zero divisor is not.

worked_examples.title: Sharing Twelve Pencils
worked_examples.scenario: A workshop has twelve pencils to share equally among three tables. How many pencils does each table get?
worked_examples.prediction: Each table gets the same number, and no pencil is left over.
step_by_step: Set out three groups, one for each table. You may imagine them instead of drawing them.
Give one pencil to each table. One round uses three pencils. After two rounds you have used six; after three rounds, nine; after four rounds, twelve.
Each table now has four pencils. Count across all groups: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
Write 12 ÷ 3 = 4 and label the result: four pencils per table.
Check: 3 × 4 = 12. All twelve pencils are accounted for, so the remainder is zero.
worked_examples.explanation: The divisor names the three tables, and the quotient names the pencils at each table. Every distribution round treats the groups equally. Nothing about the written answer requires seeing a picture; three groups of four is the same structure.
worked_examples.visual_description: Table A: four pencils. Table B: four pencils. Table C: four pencils. Three tables, each with four, contain twelve altogether.

worked_examples.title: Filling Bags with Six Counters
worked_examples.scenario: There are twenty-four counters. Each bag must contain six counters. How many full bags can you make?
worked_examples.prediction: We need the number of bags, because the number of counters in each bag is already known.
step_by_step: Identify the total: twenty-four counters. Identify the fixed group size: six counters per bag.
Ask the multiplication question: six times what number equals twenty-four?
Count equal groups if needed: 6, 12, 18, 24. Four groups of six reach the total.
Write 24 ÷ 6 = 4. The answer is four bags, not four counters in each bag.
Check by multiplying: 6 × 4 = 24. No counters remain.
worked_examples.explanation: This is equal grouping. Compare it with sharing twenty-four counters among six bags: that different story also uses 24 ÷ 6 = 4, but its answer would be four counters per bag. Units tell you what the same number sentence means in each situation.
worked_examples.visual_description: Four bags each contain six counters. The running totals after filling each bag are six, twelve, eighteen, and twenty-four.

worked_examples.title: Enough Envelopes for Every Card
worked_examples.scenario: You have twenty-three cards. An envelope holds at most five cards. How many full envelopes can you fill, how many cards remain, and how many envelopes are needed to store all the cards?
worked_examples.prediction: Twenty-three lies between twenty and twenty-five, so four envelopes will be full and another will hold the leftover cards.
step_by_step: Find nearby multiples: 5 × 4 = 20 and 5 × 5 = 25. Twenty-five is more cards than we have.
Fill four envelopes with five cards each. These envelopes contain twenty cards.
Subtract to find the remainder: 23 - 20 = 3 cards.
Check: 23 = 5 × 4 + 3, and 0 ≤ 3 < 5. The whole-number quotient is four and the remainder is three.
To store every card, use one more envelope for the remaining three. Four full envelopes plus one partly filled envelope means five envelopes in total.
worked_examples.explanation: The whole-number quotient answers how many full groups can be made. It does not always answer the practical question. Four envelopes would leave three cards outside; five envelopes hold all twenty-three. The fifth envelope need not be full. State which question you are answering.
worked_examples.visual_description: Envelopes one through four each hold five cards. Envelope five holds three cards, leaving room for two more.

exercises.title: Guided Equal Sharing
exercises.problem_statement: Share fifteen counters equally among three trays. How many counters go on each tray? Write a division sentence and a multiplication check.
exercises.hint: Distribute one counter to each tray per round. How many rounds use all fifteen?
exercises.solution: Five rounds use 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 15 counters. Each tray receives five. Therefore 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Check: 3 × 5 = 15, with zero left over.

exercises.title: Make Groups of Six
exercises.problem_statement: There are eighteen markers. Put six markers in each cup. How many cups can you fill?
exercises.hint: Subtract six at a time or find the missing number in 6 × ? = 18.
exercises.solution: Eighteen minus six is twelve; twelve minus six is six; six minus six is zero. Three groups were removed, so three cups are full. Check: 6 × 3 = 18.

exercises.title: Explain the Zero
exercises.problem_statement: Four empty trays have zero counters to share. Find 0 ÷ 4 and check it. Then explain why 8 ÷ 0 and 0 ÷ 0 do not have defined answers in ordinary arithmetic.
exercises.hint: For each division, ask what number multiplied by the divisor would give the total. Is there exactly one answer?
exercises.solution: Each of the four trays has zero counters, so 0 ÷ 4 = 0; check: 4 × 0 = 0. No number times zero equals eight, so 8 ÷ 0 has no answer. Every number times zero equals zero, so 0 ÷ 0 has no unique answer. Both expressions with a zero divisor are undefined.

exercises.title: Check a Proposed Remainder
exercises.problem_statement: A learner says: “Twenty-nine counters shared among four trays gives six per tray with five left over, because 4 × 6 + 5 = 29.” The total checks, but is this a finished division answer? Find the whole-number quotient and remainder.
exercises.hint: Can you give one of the five leftover counters to each tray?
exercises.solution: Five leftovers are enough for another full round of four. Give one more counter to each tray: six per tray becomes seven, and five leftovers become one. Check: 4 × 7 + 1 = 29. The remainder one is smaller than four. Six remainder five preserves the total but has not finished forming all possible equal groups.
exercises.answer: Seven counters per tray, one left over; 29 ÷ 4 = 7 remainder 1.

exercises.title: One Calculation, Two Questions
exercises.problem_statement: You have forty-seven beads. First, share them equally among five people without cutting beads. How many does each person receive, and what remains? Next, instead store all forty-seven beads in containers holding at most five beads each. How many containers are needed? Explain why the final answers name different things.
exercises.hint: Use 5 × 9 = 45. In the storage question, the extra beads also need a container.
exercises.solution: Forty-seven minus forty-five is two. In equal sharing, each of the five people receives nine beads, with two left over: 47 = 5 × 9 + 2. For storage, nine full containers hold forty-five beads; a tenth holds the remaining two. Nine is the number of beads per person in the first question and the number of full containers in the second. Ten is the total containers needed to hold everything.
exercises.answer: Sharing: nine beads each, two left over. Storage: ten containers, nine full and one holding two beads.

content.interactive_experience: No digital interactive lab is required. Optionally move counters or make marks on paper to form equal groups; the written descriptions provide the same information.
content.text_only_path: Read the introduction and two core sections, then work through all three examples. Try each exercise before reading its hint or solution. Explain what the quotient counts and check total = divisor × quotient + remainder. Take breaks as needed; on another day, revisit one sharing question and one grouping question. The complete text is embedded here and also provided in docs/lessons/introduction-to-division.md; external sources are optional further reading and require a connection.

sources.title: Division by Zero
sources.authors: Eric W. Weisstein, MathWorld—A Wolfram Web Resource
sources.description: Supports the explanation that division by zero is undefined for real numbers because multiplication by zero cannot be uniquely inverted. The lesson stays within ordinary whole-number arithmetic; specialized mathematical extensions are outside its scope.
